questions.q: Which of these is the best definition of master data, per this lesson?
options: The core business entities â€” customers, products, vendors, employees, locations â€” that multiple systems and processes share and reuse
Any data that is backed up to a secondary location
The raw log files generated by a web server
Data that has been deleted but not yet purged
questions.explain: Master data is defined by being the core, reusable entities an organization refers to repeatedly across many systems â€” not by backup status, log format, or deletion state.

questions.q: Per this lesson's fast test, how do you tell the three data categories apart?
options: By checking which department's budget paid for the database server
By asking whether the record describes a thing (master), an allowed value (reference), or an event (transactional)
By checking the file format the data is stored in
By checking which programming language wrote the record
questions.explain: The lesson's test is conceptual: a customer is a thing (master), a country code is an allowed value (reference), and an order is an event (transactional).

questions.q: What does the registry style of MDM architecture actually store centrally?
options: A full physical copy of every source system's master data
Only matching keys and cross-reference links between records in different source systems
Nothing â€” registry style has no central component at all
A complete rewrite of every source system's database schema
questions.explain: Registry style is the lightest touch: source data stays exactly where it is, and the central registry just maps which records across systems refer to the same real-world entity.

questions.q: What are the three governance pillars this lesson identifies for an MDM program?
options: Domain ownership, standards and rules, and stewardship workflow
Server uptime, network latency, and disk capacity
Marketing budget, sales quota, and headcount
Software license cost, vendor support tier, and renewal date
questions.explain: The lesson names domain ownership, written standards/rules, and a defined stewardship workflow as the three pillars that keep an MDM program from drifting back into chaos.

questions.q: What is matching, as defined in this lesson?
options: Backing up records to a secondary database
Comparing records, within one system or across several, to decide whether they represent the same real-world entity
Deleting duplicate records automatically without review
Encrypting sensitive fields before storage
questions.explain: Matching is the comparison process that decides whether two records refer to the same real-world thing â€” the mechanical heart of MDM.

questions.q: What is deterministic matching, as defined in this lesson?
options: Matching based on exact rules applied to specific fields â€” if they match exactly (or after simple standardization), the records are treated as the same entity
Matching based purely on random sampling of records
A method that never produces explainable results
A method that only works on image data
questions.explain: Deterministic matching is rule-based and exact â€” a defined field match (like an exact tax ID match) decides the outcome, with no scoring involved.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish deduplication from the broader matching concept in Lesson 6?
options: Deduplication is matching applied specifically within a single system or dataset, rather than across multiple systems
Deduplication and matching are completely unrelated processes
Deduplication only applies to reference data, never master data
Deduplication is a synonym for golden record creation
questions.explain: The lesson defines deduplication as the narrower case of matching, scoped to finding duplicates that already exist within one system or dataset.

questions.q: What is a golden record, as defined in this lesson?
options: The single, trusted, best-available version of a master data entity, reconciled from matched source records
A backup copy of a database stored off-site
The oldest record in a system
Any record that has never been edited
questions.explain: A golden record is the reconciled, trusted result built by comparing and merging the matched records that refer to the same real-world entity.

questions.q: What is a customer master record, as defined in this lesson?
options: The authoritative, relatively stable record of every party an organization sells to, bills, or supports
A single table of every transaction a customer has ever made
A marketing-only list of email addresses used for newsletters
The list of employees who are permitted to contact customers
questions.explain: A customer master record holds stable identifying and classification attributes â€” ID, names, addresses, tax IDs, status â€” not transactional data that changes with every order.

questions.q: What is the difference between a product and a SKU, as explained in this lesson?
options: A product is the conceptual item; a SKU is one specific sellable variant of it with its own barcode and inventory count
A product and a SKU are two words for exactly the same thing
A SKU is always a higher-level grouping than a product
A product only exists in e-commerce, while a SKU only exists in warehouses
questions.explain: 'Men's Crew Socks, Size M' is the product; 'Men's Crew Socks, Size M, Black, 3-Pack' is a SKU â€” one of possibly many variants under that product.

questions.q: What is a vendor (supplier) master record, as defined in this lesson?
options: The authoritative record of every external party an organization pays for goods or services
A record of every customer who has ever purchased from the organization
A log of every email sent to external partners
A list of employees authorized to approve purchase orders
questions.explain: Vendor master mirrors customer master in structure, but tracks parties the organization pays rather than parties that pay the organization.

questions.q: What distinguishes a fixed-level hierarchy from a recursive hierarchy?
options: A fixed-level hierarchy always has the same number of levels for every record; a recursive hierarchy has variable depth
A fixed-level hierarchy only applies to employees, never to products
A recursive hierarchy cannot be used for reporting roll-ups
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Brand to category to product is always exactly four levels (fixed), while a corporate family tree can be two levels for one customer and six for another (recursive).

questions.q: How does this lesson define reference data?
options: A small, stable, finite list of valid values used to classify or constrain other data
Any data stored in a relational database table
The full set of a customer's past orders
A backup copy of master data kept for disaster recovery
questions.explain: Reference data is the controlled vocabulary â€” like country codes or status codes â€” that other data is classified against, distinct from master data (entities) and transactional data (events).

questions.q: What are the three lifecycle stages a code list value goes through, according to this lesson?
options: Added, deprecated, retired
Encrypted, hashed, archived
Imported, exported, compressed
Created, renamed, duplicated
questions.explain: Codes are added when a new valid value is needed, deprecated when no longer usable for new records (but still referenced historically), and retired when fully removed from active use.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say reference data governance needs its own mechanics, separate from master data governance?
options: Because a reference data change can silently affect every system that stores the changed code, unlike a master data change affecting one record
Because reference data is never actually governed in practice
Because reference data changes require no approval of any kind
Because reference data is always larger in volume than master data
questions.explain: Updating one customer's address affects that record; redefining what a status code means can ripple across every transactional system that stores that code.

questions.q: What is a cross-reference (mapping) table, as defined in this lesson?
options: A table that translates between two or more systems' code lists without requiring either one to change
A table that merges two systems into a single combined database
A list of every employee who has access to reference data
A backup copy of a master data table
questions.explain: Rather than forcing one system to adopt the other's codes, a cross-reference table holds both systems' codes side by side so integrations can translate between them.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff between batch and real-time master data distribution, per this lesson?
options: Batch is simpler but leaves consumers stale between runs; real-time is more complex but avoids staleness where it would cause real harm
Batch distribution is always faster than real-time distribution
Real-time distribution requires no infrastructure at all
Batch distribution can only be used for customer master, never for other domains
questions.explain: Batch is acceptable for most reference and master data, but real-time is reserved for cases like a customer's credit hold status, where a delay could cause an order to ship that shouldn't.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a quality problem in master data worse than one in a one-off report?
options: Because master data is shared, so a single wrong value flows out to every downstream system that consumes it
Because master data is always stored in a slower database
Because master data has no owner by definition
Because reports are never checked for accuracy at all
questions.explain: A wrong value in master data isn't contained to one place â€” it's distributed to every consuming system (CRM, billing, support, marketing), so one error becomes many.

questions.q: In the registry MDM style, what does the hub actually hold?
options: An index of pointers and match keys, not full golden records
A complete copy of every record from every source system
Nothing at all â€” registry style has no hub
Only reference data code lists, never master data
questions.explain: Registry style keeps the hub lightweight â€” it points to where the authoritative record lives in each source system rather than storing full golden records centrally.

questions.q: What reference data problem did the Chapter 4 step of the walkthrough fix?
options: Three systems used different codes for the same country or state/province (e.g. CA, CAN, and the spelled-out name), now unified under one governed code list
The company had no product catalog of any kind
All vendor records had already been perfectly deduplicated before this step
Reference data was deemed unnecessary and removed entirely
questions.explain: Drifted local code lists for country/state values were replaced with one managed, governed code list, with cross-reference tables mapping legacy codes during the transition.
